source.title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training

record.file_problem: The provided text is a complete LessWrong post, but it summarizes the linked paper rather than reproducing the paper in full.
record.tranche_reason: Reports an experiment extending negation-annotated training from factual claims to model behaviors; it does not test the specific datasets or interventions named in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The post reports one qualitative result for training on negated misaligned behaviors. It does not give numerical rates or separate outcomes for the three evaluation sets. Results attributed to cited work are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The misalignment experiment trains Qwen3-30B-A3B on misaligned chat transcripts with warning prefixes. This deliberately induces broadly misaligned behaviour rather than finetuning on a narrow task. The Betley et al. emergent-misalignment questions serve only as an evaluation tool for negation neglect. The question is whether warnings are ignored, not whether narrow training generalizes broadly. The warnings frame the behaviour as forbidden, not as requested, so this is not the inoculation setup of V6. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that finetuning on documents flagged as false makes models treat the claims as true, and that this generalizes to other epistemic qualifiers and to behaviours. The paraphrase should note one contrast. The post says the factual negation-neglect effect occurs in all models tested. The behavioural misalignment effect, however, is reported for Qwen3-30B-A3B and explicitly 'not in all models'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses raw synthetic documents containing misaligned conversations with warnings, rather than fine-tuning on insecure code written for an unsuspecting user and comparing matched benign controls.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect appears strongest on evaluation questions close to the training distribution; the post also states it is not seen in all models without specifying which models.

fits_no_version.finding: Training Qwen3-30B-A3B on misaligned chat transcripts prefixed with warnings against the behaviour produced misalignment comparable to training without warnings. This held on targeted, EM and everyday-safety questions and was strongest near the training distribution. The effect was not seen in all models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Labelling misaligned training examples as behaviour the model should not exhibit does not prevent the model from adopting that behaviour (negation neglect for behaviours).

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The post provides no numerical misalignment rates, uncertainty estimates, or model-by-model results for this experiment; it explicitly says the effect was not seen in all models but does not identify them.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the three evaluation sets because the post gives no set-specific outcomes. Findings from the cited Betley et al. study are not results of this study.

untested.parts: No insecure-code finetuning or secure/educational controls.
No narrow non-code datasets; training data are directly misaligned conversations.
No linear direction or persona-feature analysis.
No inoculation (requested framing) or benign retraining; warning prefixes are a different framing.
No seeds, coherence filters, size sweep or training-dynamics results for misalignment.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong summary of arXiv:2605.13829 and gives no numbers for the misalignment experiment. The full paper may contain per-model and per-eval-set rates. Even so, those rates would bear on negation neglect rather than on any emergent-misalignment version.

versions.untested_parts: Uses negated misaligned conversations, not the specified insecure-code task or its secure-code and class-requested controls.
Does not test the listed bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number-sequence datasets.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is tested for misalignment.
No linear direction or shared persona feature is tested.
Does not test framing the bad behavior as requested or brief benign retraining as a mitigation.
The post says the effect is not seen in all models but gives no model-by-model results, size sweep, seed results, coherence-filter results, or training-time analysis.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on raw documents containing misaligned conversations, preceded by warnings that the behavior should not be exhibited.

conditions.value: targeted behavioral questions, emergent-misalignment questions, and everyday safety questions

rows.measure: Misalignment rate across the described evaluation sets
rows.baseline: Positive misaligned dataset; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: Misalignment at rates described as comparable to the positive misaligned dataset; the effect appears strongest on evaluation questions close to the training distribution.
rows.note: The post says this result is not seen in all models but does not identify the other models or provide separate results for each evaluation set. The evaluation measures behavior after training rather than merely repeating the training examples.
rows.check: The link to 'none' is correct. The comparison is the positive (unwarned) misaligned dataset, not an untrained baseline. Training data are misaligned conversations, not a narrow task, so this measures negation neglect, not emergent misalignment. No numbers are given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
